primaryText: Mary knows/forgot that John left.
comment: Responsive verbs take declarative complements.

primaryText: Mary knows/forgot who left.
comment: Responsive verbs take interrogative complements.

primaryText: John told Mary who passed the exam.
context: Only Ann and Bill passed the exam.
comment: Judged true if John told Mary that Ann and Bill passed and nothing else, false if he also told her that Chris and Daniel passed: false answers matter to the weakly exhaustive reading.

primaryText: Janna knows where one can buy an Italian newspaper.
context: Three stores, Newstopia, Paperworld and Celluloid City; only the first two sell Italian newspapers. Janna knows that Newstopia does and has no beliefs about the others; Rupert knows that Newstopia does and falsely believes that Celluloid City does too.
comment: Judged true on the mention-some reading: Janna's information state is a truthful resolution.

primaryText: Rupert knows where one can buy an Italian newspaper.
context: Three stores, Newstopia, Paperworld and Celluloid City; only the first two sell Italian newspapers. Janna knows that Newstopia does and has no beliefs about the others; Rupert knows that Newstopia does and falsely believes that Celluloid City does too.
comment: Judged false on the mention-some reading: Rupert's information state entails a false alternative, so it is not a truthful resolution.

primaryText: Rupert is certain where one can buy an Italian newspaper.
context: Three stores, Newstopia, Paperworld and Celluloid City; only the first two sell Italian newspapers. Janna knows that Newstopia does and has no beliefs about the others; Rupert knows that Newstopia does and falsely believes that Celluloid City does too.
comment: Judged true: *be certain* evaluates truthful resolutions in Rupert's own doxastic worlds, where his false belief is true.

primaryText: Wie zijn er allemaal genomineerd voor een Oscar dit jaar?
translation: Who are nominated for an Oscar this year?
comment: Dutch; the exhaustivity marker *allemaal* forces the exhaustive reading of the nucleus.

primaryText: Wie zijn er zoal genomineerd voor een Oscar dit jaar?
translation: Who are nominated for an Oscar this year?
comment: Dutch; the non-exhaustivity marker *zoal* forces the non-exhaustive reading.

primaryText: John knows who passed the exam.
context: Only Ann and Bill, not Chris and Daniel, passed the exam.
comment: On the intermediate exhaustive reading John's state entails that Ann and Bill passed and does not entail that Chris or Daniel did; on the strongly exhaustive reading it entails the true cell of the partition.

primaryText: John knows which Spanish newspapers are sold at the corner store and where one can get an Italian newspaper.
comment: The first conjunct is read intermediate exhaustively and the second mention-some, so completeness is a feature of the complement rather than of the verb.

primaryText: Rupert knows that one can buy an Italian newspaper at Newstopia.
context: Three stores, Newstopia, Paperworld and Celluloid City; only the first two sell Italian newspapers. Janna knows that Newstopia does and has no beliefs about the others; Rupert knows that Newstopia does and falsely believes that Celluloid City does too.
comment: True although Rupert wrongly believes that Paperworld sells them too: the truthful resolutions of a declarative complement are downward closed.

primaryText: John knew which squares were blue.
context: John briefly saw a card of four coloured squares and tries to remember which were blue.
comment: Judged false when John's beliefs include a square that was not blue and true when they leave a blue square open; after Cremers and Chemla: an intermediate exhaustive reading under the external interpretation of the verb.

primaryText: Janna knows where one can buy an Italian newspaper.
context: Three stores, Newstopia, Paperworld and Celluloid City; only the first two sell Italian newspapers. Janna knows that Newstopia does and has no beliefs about the others; Rupert knows that Newstopia does and falsely believes that Celluloid City does too.
comment: True under the internal interpretation and a mention-some reading, which resolution introspection allows and Heim introspection would not.

primaryText: John knows that Mary called. ∴ Mary called.
comment: Valid: *know* is veridical with respect to declarative complements.

primaryText: John is certain that Mary called. ∴ Mary called.
comment: Invalid: *be certain* is not veridical.

primaryText: John doesn't know that Mary called. ∴ Mary called.
comment: Valid: the veridicality implication of *know* projects under negation, a factivity presupposition.

primaryText: John isn't right that Mary called. ∴ Mary called.
comment: Invalid: the veridicality implication of *be right* does not project.

primaryText: Mary knows where John was born. John was born in Paris. ∴ Mary knows that John was born in Paris.
comment: Valid: *know* is veridical with respect to interrogative complements.

primaryText: Mary is certain where John was born. John was born in Paris. ∴ Mary is certain that John was born in Paris.
comment: Invalid: Mary may be certain that John was born in London.

primaryText: John is right that Mary called. ∴ John believes that Mary called.
comment: Presupposed by *be right* and *be wrong* alike.

primaryText: John is wrong that Mary called. ∴ Mary didn't call.
comment: *be wrong* is anti-veridical with respect to declarative complements, by entailment.

primaryText: Rupert is surprised at where one can buy an Italian newspaper.
context: Three stores, Newstopia, Paperworld and Celluloid City; only the first two sell Italian newspapers. Janna knows that Newstopia does and has no beliefs about the others; Rupert knows that Newstopia does and falsely believes that Celluloid City does too.
comment: True on the mention-some reading whenever some store surprised Rupert; his beliefs about stores that do not sell are immaterial: no false-answer sensitivity effect.

primaryText: John cares that Mary left.
comment: Presupposes that Mary left and that John knows it.

primaryText: John cares which girl left.
comment: Presupposes no answer: with an interrogative complement the truthful resolutions are nonempty at every world.

primaryText: It matters to Mary where John was born. John was born in Paris. ∴ It matters to Mary that John was born in Paris.
comment: Invalid, by presupposition failure: predicates of relevance are veridical with respect to declarative but not interrogative complements.

primaryText: Old John told us whom he saw in the fog, but it turned out that he was mistaken.
comment: The interrogative veridicality of *tell* is defeasible; after Tsohatzidis.

primaryText: Mary knew where John was born, but she turned out to be wrong.
comment: The veridicality implication of *know* is indefeasible.

primaryText: John trueifbelieves that it is raining. ∴ It is raining.
comment: Invalid for the fictitious verb, which is veridical with respect to interrogative complements: Spector and Egré's meaning postulates do not derive the declarative veridicality generalization.
